entries.29038daa004698cf2304472105d921b9d8d832e1: <div sID="gen7642" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="1Chr.4" sID="1Chr.4"/> <div eID="gen7642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7643" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7644" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. A further account of the genealogies of the tribe of Judah, the most numerous and most famous of all the tribes. The posterity of Shobal the son of Hur (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.1-1Chr.4.4">ver. 1-4</reference>), of Ashur the posthumous son of Hezron (who was mentioned, <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.24">ii. 24</reference>), with something particular concerning Jabez (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.5-1Chr.4.10">ver. 5-10</reference>), of Chelub and others (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.11-1Chr.4.20">ver. 11-20</reference>), of Shelah, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.21-1Chr.4.23">ver. 21-23</reference>. II. An account of the posterity and cities of Simeon, their conquest of Gedon, and of the Amalekites in Mount Seir, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.24-1Chr.4.43">ver. 24-43</reference>.
entries.720b699b163902ecfbde13edfe6e1c232d36045b: <div eID="gen7644" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7643" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sons of Judah; The Prayer of Jabez. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1720.)</title> <div sID="gen7645" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The sons of Judah; Pharez, Hezron, and Carmi, and Hur, and Shobal. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Reaiah the son of Shobal begat Jahath; and Jahath begat Ahumai, and Lahad. These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the families of the Zorathites. <hi type="super">3</hi> And these <hi type="italic">were of</hi> the father of Etam; Jezreel, and Ishma, and Idbash: and the name of their sister <hi type="italic">was</hi> Hazelel-poni: <hi type="super">4</hi> And Penuel the father of Gedor, and Ezer the father of Hushah. These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah, the father of Bethlehem. <hi type="super">5</hi> And Ashur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah. <hi type="super">6</hi> And Naarah bare him Ahuzam, and Hepher, and Temeni, and Haahashtari. These <hi type="italic">were</hi> the sons of Naarah. <hi type="super">7</hi> And the sons of Helah <hi type="italic">were,</hi> Zereth, and Jezoar, and Ethnan. <hi type="super">8</hi> And Coz begat Anub, and Zobebah, and the families of Aharhel the son of Harum. <hi type="super">9</hi> And Jabez was more honourable than his brethren: and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, Because I bare him with sorrow. <hi type="super">10</hi> And Jabez called on the God of Israel, saying, Oh that thou wouldest bless me indeed, and enlarge my coast, and that thine hand might be with me, and that thou wouldest keep <hi type="italic">me</hi> from evil, that it may not grieve me! And God granted him that which he requested. <div eID="gen7645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7646" type="x-p"/> One reason, no doubt, why Ezra is here most particular in the register of the tribe of Judah is because it was that tribe which, with its appendages, Simeon, Benjamin, and Levi, made up the kingdom of Judah, which not only long survived the other tribes in Canaan, but in process of time, now when this was written, returned out of captivity, when the generality of the other tribes were lost in the kingdom of Assyria. The most remarkable person in this paragraph is Jabez. It is not said whose son he was, nor does it appear in what age he lived; but, it should seem, he was the founder of one of the families of Aharhel, mentioned <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.8">v. 8</reference>. Here is, <div eID="gen7646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7647" type="x-p"/> I. The reason of his name: his mother gave him the name with this reason, <hi type="italic">Because I bore him with sorrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.9">v. 9</reference>. All children are borne with sorrow (for the sentence upon the woman is, <hi type="italic">In sorrow shalt thou bring forth children</hi>), but some with much more sorrow than others. Usually the sorrow in bearing is afterwards forgotten <hi type="italic">for joy that the child is born;</hi> but here it seems it was so extraordinary that it was remembered when the child came to be circumcised, and care was taken to perpetuate the remembrance of it while he lived. Perhaps the mother called Habez, as Rachel called her son Benoni, when she was dying of the sorrow. Or, if she recovered it, yet thus she recorded it, 1. That it might be a continual memorandum to herself, to be thankful to God as long as she lived for supporting her under and bringing her through that sorrow. It may be of use to be often reminded of our sorrows, that we may always have such thoughts of things as we had in the day of our affliction, and may learn to rejoice with trembling. 2. That it might likewise be a memorandum to him what this world is into which she bore him, a vale of tears, in which he must expect <hi type="italic">few days and full of trouble.</hi> The sorrow he carried in his name might help to put a seriousness upon his spirit. It might also remind him to love and honour his mother, and labour, in every thing, to be a comfort to her who brought him into the world with so much sorrow. It is piety in children thus to requite their parents, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.4">1 Tim. v. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen7647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7648" type="x-p"/> II. The eminence of his character: <hi type="italic">He was more honourable than his brethren,</hi> qualified above them by the divine grace and dignified above them by the divine providence; they did virtuously, but he excelled them all. Now the sorrow with which his mother bore him was abundantly recompensed. That son which of all her children cost her most dear she was most happy in, and was made glad in proportion to the affliction, <reference osisRef="Ps.90.15">Ps. xc. 15</reference>. We are not told upon what account he was <hi type="italic">more honourable than his brethren,</hi> whether because he raised a greater estate, or was preferred to the magistracy, or signalized himself in war; we have most reason to think it was upon the account of his learning and piety, not only because these, above any thing, put honour upon a man, but because we have reason to think that in these Jabez was eminent. 1. In learning, because we find that <hi type="italic">the families of the scribes dwelt at Jabez</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.55">ch. ii. 55</reference>), a city which, it is likely, took its name from him. The Jews say that he was a famous doctor of the law and left many disciples behind him. And it should seem, by the mentioning of him so abruptly here, that his name was well known when Ezra wrote this. 2. In piety, because we find here that he was a praying man. His inclination to devotion made him truly honourable, and by prayer he obtained those blessings from God which added much to his honour. The way to be truly great is to be truly good and to pray much. <div eID="gen7648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7649" type="x-p"/> III. The prayer he made, probably like Solomon's prayer for wisdom, just when he was setting out in the world. He set himself to acknowledge God in all his ways, put himself under the divine blessing and protection, and prospered accordingly. Perhaps these were the heads on which he enlarged in his daily prayers; for this purpose it was his constant practice to pray alone, and with his family, as Daniel. Some think that it was upon some particular occasion, when he was straitened and threatened by his enemies, that he prayed this prayer. Observe, <div eID="gen7649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7650" type="x-p"/> 1. To whom he prayed, not to any of the gods of the Gentiles; no, he <hi type="italic">called on the God of Israel,</hi> the living and true God, who alone can hear and answer prayer, and in prayer had an eye to him as the God of Israel, a God in covenant with his people, the God with whom Jacob wrestled and prevailed and was thence called Israel. <div eID="gen7650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7651" type="x-p"/> 2. What was the nature of his prayer. (1.) As the <hi type="italic">margin</hi> reads it, it was a solemn vow—<hi type="italic">If thou wilt bless me indeed, &c.</hi> and then the sense is imperfect, but may easily be filled up from Jacob's vow, or some such like—<hi type="italic">then thou shalt be my God.</hi> He did not express his promise, but left it to be understood, either because he was afraid to promise in his own strength or because he resolved to devote himself entirely to God. He does, as it were, give God a blank paper, let him write what he pleases: "Lord, if thou wilt bless me and keep me, do what thou wilt with me, I will be at thy command and disposal for ever." (2.) As the <hi type="italic">text</hi> reads it, it was the language of a most ardent and affectionate desire: <hi type="italic">O that thou wouldst bless me!</hi> <div eID="gen7651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7652" type="x-p"/> 3. What was the matter of his prayer. Four things he prayed for:—(1.) That God would bless him indeed: "That, <hi type="italic">blessing, thou wilt bless me,</hi> bless me greatly with manifold and abundant blessings." Perhaps he had an eye to the promise God made to Abraham (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.17">Gen. xxii. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">In blessing, I will bless thee.</hi> "Let that blessing of Abraham come upon me." Spiritual blessings are the best blessings, and those are blessed indeed who are blessed with them. God's blessings are real things and produce real effects. We can but wish a blessing: he commands it. Those whom he blesses are blessed indeed. (2.) That he would enlarge his coast, that he would prosper his endeavours for the increase of what fell to his lot either by work or war. That God would enlarge our hearts, and so enlarge our portion in himself and in the heavenly Canaan, ought to be our desire and prayer. (3.) That God's hand might be with him. The prayer of Moses for this tribe of Judah was, That his own <hi type="italic">hands might be sufficient for him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.7">Deut. xxxiii. 7</reference>; but Jabez expects not that this can be the case, unless he have <hi type="italic">God's</hi> hand with him and the presence of his power. God's hand with us, to lead us, protect us, strengthen us, and to work all our works in us and for us, is indeed a hand sufficient for us, all-sufficient. (4.) That he would keep him from evil, the evil of sin, the evil of trouble, all the evil designs of his enemies, that they might not hurt him, nor grieve him, nor make him a <hi type="italic">Jabez</hi> indeed, <hi type="italic">a man of sorrow:</hi> in the original there is an allusion to his name. <hi type="italic">Father in heaven, deliver me from evil.</hi> <div eID="gen7652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7653" type="x-p"/> 4. What was the success of his prayer: <hi type="italic">God granted him that which he requested,</hi> prospered him remarkably, and gave him success in his undertakings, in his studies, in his worldly business, in his conflicts with the Canaanites, and so he became <hi type="italic">more honourable than his brethren.</hi> God was of old always ready to hear prayer, and <hi type="italic">his ear is not yet heavy.</hi>
entries.3e1b74f37fb17bf46907f06c22d59e9a8d26dd05: <div eID="gen7653" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Genealogies. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1420.)</title> <div sID="gen7654" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> And Chelub the brother of Shuah begat Mehir, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> the father of Eshton. <hi type="super">12</hi> And Eshton begat Beth-rapha, and Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Irnahash. These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the men of Rechah. <hi type="super">13</hi> And the sons of Kenaz; Othniel, and Seraiah: and the sons of Othniel; Hathath. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Meonothai begat Ophrah: and Seraiah begat Joab, the father of the valley of Charashim; for they were craftsmen. <hi type="super">15</hi> And the sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh; Iru, Elah, and Naam: and the sons of Elah, even Kenaz. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the sons of Jehaleleel; Ziph, and Ziphah, Tiria, and Asareel. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the sons of Ezra <hi type="italic">were,</hi> Jether, and Mered, and Epher, and Jalon: and she bare Miriam, and Shammai, and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa. <hi type="super">18</hi> And his wife Jehudijah bare Jered the father of Gedor, and Heber the father of Socho, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. And these <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the sons of <hi type="italic">his</hi> wife Hodiah the sister of Naham, the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite. <hi type="super">20</hi> And the sons of Shimon <hi type="italic">were,</hi> Amnon, and Rinnah, Benhanan, and Tilon. And the sons of Ishi <hi type="italic">were,</hi> Zoheth, and Benzoheth. <hi type="super">21</hi> The sons of Shelah the son of Judah <hi type="italic">were,</hi> Er the father of Lecah, and Laadah the father of Mareshah, and the families of the house of them that wrought fine linen, of the house of Ashbea, <hi type="super">22</hi> And Jokim, and the men of Chozeba, and Joash, and Saraph, who had the dominion in Moab, and Jashubilehem. And <hi type="italic">these are</hi> ancient things. <hi type="super">23</hi> These <hi type="italic">were</hi> the potters, and those that dwelt among plants and hedges: there they dwelt with the king for his work. <div eID="gen7654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7655" type="x-p"/> We may observe in these verses, 1. That here is a whole family of craftsmen, handicraft tradesmen, that applied themselves to all sorts of manufactures, in which they were ingenious and industrious above their neighbours, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.14">v. 14</reference>. There was a valley where they lived which was, from them, called <hi type="italic">the valley of craftsmen.</hi> Those that are craftsmen are not therefore to be looked upon as mean men. These craftsmen, though two of a trade often disagree, yet chose to live together, for the improving of arts by comparing notes, and that they might support one another's reputation. 2. That one of these married the daughter of Pharaoh (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.18">v. 18</reference>), which was the common name of the kings of Egypt. If an Israelite in Egypt before the bondage began, while Joseph's merits were yet fresh in mind, was preferred to be the king's son-in-law, it is not to be thought strange: few Israelites could, like Moses, refuse an alliance with the court. 3. That another is said to be the <hi type="italic">father of the house of those that wrought fine linen,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.21">v. 21</reference>. It is inserted in their genealogy as their honour that they were the best weavers in the kingdom, and they brought up their children, from one generation to another, to the same business, not aiming to make them gentlemen. This Laadah is said to be the <hi type="italic">father of those that wrought fine linen,</hi> as before the flood Jubal is said to be <hi type="italic">the father of musicians</hi> and Jabal of <hi type="italic">shepherds,</hi> &c. His posterity inhabited the city of Mareshah, the manufacture or staple commodity of which place was linen-cloth, with which their kings and priests were clothed. 4. That another family had had <hi type="italic">dominion in Moab,</hi> but were now in <hi type="italic">servitude in Babylon,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.22-1Chr.4.23">v. 22, 23</reference>. (1.) It was found among the <hi type="italic">ancient things</hi> that they had the <hi type="italic">dominion in Moab.</hi> Probably in David's time, when that country was conquered, they transplanted themselves thither, and were put in places of power there, which they held for several generations; but this was a great while ago, time out of mind. (2.) Their posterity were now potters and gardeners, as is supposed in Babylon, where they <hi type="italic">dwelt with the king for his work,</hi> got a good livelihood by their industry, and therefore cared not for returning with their brethren to their own land, after the years of captivity had expired. Those that now have dominion know not what their posterity may be reduced to, nor what mean employments they may be glad to take up with. But those were unworthy the name of <hi type="italic">Israelites</hi> that would dwell among <hi type="italic">plants and hedges</hi> rather than be at the pains to return to Canaan.
entries.63ea9ef03b4bb6bbf53389b79e9d620444296012: <div eID="gen7655" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Genealogies. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 715.)</title> <div sID="gen7656" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> The sons of Simeon <hi type="italic">were,</hi> Nemuel, and Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, <hi type="italic">and</hi> Shaul: <hi type="super">25</hi> Shallum his son, Mibsam his son, Mishma his son. <hi type="super">26</hi> And the sons of Mishma; Hamuel his son, Zacchur his son, Shimei his son. <hi type="super">27</hi> And Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters; but his brethren had not many children, neither did all their family multiply, like to the children of Judah. <hi type="super">28</hi> And they dwelt at Beer-sheba, and Moladah, and Hazar-shual, <hi type="super">29</hi> And at Bilhah, and at Ezem, and at Tolad, <hi type="super">30</hi> And at Bethuel, and at Hormah, and at Ziklag, <hi type="super">31</hi> And at Beth-marcaboth, and Hazar-susim, and at Beth-birei, and at Shaaraim. These <hi type="italic">were</hi> their cities unto the reign of David. <hi type="super">32</hi> And their villages <hi type="italic">were,</hi> Etam, and Ain, Rimmon, and Tochen, and Ashan, five cities: <hi type="super">33</hi> And all their villages that <hi type="italic">were</hi> round about the same cities, unto Baal. These <hi type="italic">were</hi> their habitations, and their genealogy. <hi type="super">34</hi> And Meshobab, and Jamlech, and Joshah the son of Amaziah, <hi type="super">35</hi> And Joel, and Jehu the son of Josibiah, the son of Seraiah, the son of Asiel, <hi type="super">36</hi> And Elioenai, and Jaakobah, and Jeshohaiah, and Asaiah, and Adiel, and Jesimiel, and Benaiah, <hi type="super">37</hi> And Ziza the son of Shiphi, the son of Allon, the son of Jedaiah, the son of Shimri, the son of Shemaiah; <hi type="super">38</hi> These mentioned by <hi type="italic">their</hi> names <hi type="italic">were</hi> princes in their families: and the house of their fathers increased greatly. <hi type="super">39</hi> And they went to the entrance of Gedor, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks. <hi type="super">40</hi> And they found fat pasture and good, and the land <hi type="italic">was</hi> wide, and quiet, and peaceable; for <hi type="italic">they</hi> of Ham had dwelt there of old. <hi type="super">41</hi> And these written by name came in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and smote their tents, and the habitations that were found there, and destroyed them utterly unto this day, and dwelt in their rooms: because <hi type="italic">there was</hi> pasture there for their flocks. <hi type="super">42</hi> And <hi type="italic">some</hi> of them, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the sons of Simeon, five hundred men, went to mount Seir, having for their captains Pelatiah, and Neariah, and Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi. <hi type="super">43</hi> And they smote the rest of the Amalekites that were escaped, and dwelt there unto this day. <div eID="gen7656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7657" type="x-p"/> We have here some of the genealogies of the tribe of Simeon (though it was not a tribe of great note), especially the princes of that tribe, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.38">v. 38</reference>. Of this tribe it is said that they <hi type="italic">increased greatly,</hi> but <hi type="italic">not like the children of Judah,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.27">v. 27</reference>. Those whom God increases ought to be thankful, though they see others that are more increased. Here observe, 1. The cities allotted them (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.28">v. 28</reference>), of which see <reference osisRef="Josh.19.1-Josh.19.9">Joshua xix. 1</reference>, &c. When it is said that they were theirs <hi type="italic">unto the reign of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.31">v. 31</reference>) intimation is given that when the ten tribes revolted from the house of David many of the Simeonites quitted these cities, because they lay within Judah, and seated themselves elsewhere. 2. The ground they got elsewhere. When those of this tribe that revolted from the house of David were carried captive with the rest into Assyria those that adhered to Judah were remarkably owned of God and prospered in their endeavours to enlarge their coasts. It was in the days of Hezekiah that a generation of Simeonites, whose tribe had long crouched and truckled, was animated to make these bold efforts. (1.) Some of them attacked a place in Arabia, as it should seem, called <hi type="italic">the entrance of Gedor,</hi> inhabited by the posterity of accursed Ham (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.40">v. 40</reference>), made themselves masters of it, and dwelt there. This adds to the glory of Hezekiah's pious reign, that, as his kingdom in general prospered, so did particular families. It is said that they found fat pastures, and yet <hi type="italic">the land was quiet;</hi> even when the kings of Assyria were giving disturbance to all their neighbours this land escaped their alarms. The inhabitants being shepherds, who molested none, were not themselves molested, till the Simeonites came and drove them out and succeeded them, not only in the plenty, but in the peace, of their land. Those who dwell (as we do) in a fruitful country, and whose land is wide, and quiet, and peaceable, have reason to own themselves indebted to that God who <hi type="italic">appoints the bounds of our habitation.</hi> (2.) Others of them, to the number of 500, under the command of four brethren here named, made a descent upon Mount Seir, and smote the remainder of the devoted Amalekites, and took possession of their country, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.42-1Chr.4.43">v. 42, 43</reference>. Now the curses on Ham and Amalek had a further accomplishment, when they seemed dormant, if not dead; as had also the curse on Simeon, that he should be divided and scattered (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.7">Gen. xlix. 7</reference>): yet to him it was turned into a blessing, for the families of Simeon, which thus transplanted themselves into those distant countries, are said to <hi type="italic">dwell there unto this day</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.43">v. 43</reference>), by which it should seem they escaped the calamities of the captivity. Providence sometimes sends those out of trouble that are designed for preservation.  <chapter eID="1Chr.4"/> <div eID="gen7657" type="x-p"/>

entries.4181e6e19689bfc0d0a10bc2173cfb42ed747d50: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3655"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen5231" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.1-1Chr.4.8">1Ch 4:1-8</reference>. Posterity of Judah by Caleb the Son of Hur.<div eID="gen5231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5232" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3655"/><hi type="bold">1. the sons of Judah--</hi>that is, "the descendants," for with the exception of Pharez, none of those here mentioned were his immediate sons. Indeed, the others are mentioned solely to introduce the name of Shobal, whose genealogy the historian intended to trace (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.52">1Ch 2:52</reference>).<div eID="gen5232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5233" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.9-1Chr.4.20">1Ch 4:9-20</reference>. Of Jabez, and His Prayer. <div eID="gen5233" type="x-p"/>
entries.c80947decf5ae752c60f3e20242cb0153ba947de: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3656"/><div sID="gen5234" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3656"/><hi type="bold">9-10. Jabez--</hi>was, as many think, the son of Coz, or Kenaz, and is here eulogized for his sincere and fervent piety, as well, perhaps, as for some public and patriotic works which he performed. The Jewish writers affirm that he was an eminent doctor in the law, whose reputation drew so many scribes around him that a town was called by his name (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.55">1Ch 2:55</reference>); and to the piety of his character this passage bears ample testimony. The memory of the critical circumstances which marked his birth was perpetuated in his name (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.35.15">Ge 35:15</reference>); and yet, in the development of his high talents or distinguished worth in later life, his mother must have found a satisfaction and delight that amply compensated for all her early trials. His prayer which is here recorded, and which, like Jacob's, is in the form of a vow (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.20">Ge 28:20</reference>), seems to have been uttered when he was entering on an important or critical service, for the successful execution of which he placed confidence neither on his own nor his people's prowess, but looked anxiously for the aid and blessing of God. The enterprise was in all probability the expulsion of the Canaanites from the territory he occupied; and as this was a war of extermination, which God Himself had commanded, His blessing could be the more reasonably asked and expected in preserving them from all the evils to which the undertaking might expose him. In these words, "that it may not grieve me," and which might be more literally rendered, "that I may have no more sorrow," there is an allusion to the meaning of his name, Jabez, signifying "grief"; and the import of this petition is, Let me not experience the grief which my name implies, and which my sins may well produce. <div eID="gen5234" type="x-p"/>
entries.e1d4e3b55da339a62a81e77e2c07f6b0c133bfac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3658"/><div sID="gen5236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3658"/><hi type="bold">13. the sons of Kenaz--</hi>the grandfather of Caleb, who from that relationship is called a Kenezite (<reference osisRef="Num.32.12">Nu 32:12</reference>). <div eID="gen5236" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ea67c8f68579bbcf3b7326da138caaddb2afe8e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3659"/><div sID="gen5237" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3659"/><hi type="bold">14. Joab, the father of the valley of Carashim--</hi>literally, "the father of the inhabitants of the valley"--"the valley of craftsmen," as the word denotes. They dwelt together, according to a custom which, independently of any law, extensively prevails in Eastern countries for persons of the same trade to inhabit the same street or the same quarter, and to follow the same occupation from father to son, through many generations. Their occupation was probably that of carpenters, and the valley where they lived seems to have been in the neighborhood of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Neh.11.35">Ne 11:35</reference>). <div eID="gen5237" type="x-p"/>
entries.62dd0a5ee1ba2b5fa0fb3cb9294d1be4b554cd34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3660"/><div sID="gen5238" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3660"/><hi type="bold">17-18. she bare Miriam--</hi>It is difficult, as the verses stand at present, to see who is meant. The following readjustment of the text clears away the obscurity: "These are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took, and she bare Miriam, and his wife Jehudijah bare Jezreel," &c. <div eID="gen5238" type="x-p"/>
entries.30e0d92df8e9f19d7dd0800dc36fc2bb0dbc16df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3662"/><div sID="gen5241" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3662"/><hi type="bold">21. Laadah ... the father ... of the house of them that wrought fine linen--</hi>Here, again, is another incidental evidence that in very early times certain trades were followed by particular families among the Hebrews, apparently in hereditary succession. Their knowledge of the art of linen manufacture had been, most probably, acquired in Egypt, where the duty of bringing up families to the occupations of their forefathers was a compulsory obligation, whereas in Israel, as in many parts of Asia to this day, it was optional, though common. <div eID="gen5241" type="x-p"/>
entries.2cf05edf5096173421f7607d8e8324d0c7658e49: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3663"/><div sID="gen5242" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3663"/><hi type="bold">22-23. had the dominion in Moab, and Jashubi-lehem--</hi>"And these are ancient things" seems a strange rendering of a proper name; and, besides, it conveys a meaning that has no bearing on the record. The following improved translation has been suggested: "Sojourned in Moab, but returned to Beth-lehem and Adaberim-athekim. These and the inhabitants of Netaim and Gedera were potters employed by the king in his own work." Gedera or Gederoth, and Netaim, belonged to the tribe of Judah, and lay on the southeast border of the Philistines' territory (<reference osisRef="Josh.15.36">Jos 15:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.18">2Ch 28:18</reference>).<div eID="gen5242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5243" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.24-1Chr.4.43">1Ch 4:24-43</reference>. Of Simeon. <div eID="gen5243" type="x-p"/>
entries.7949e51547d08d04b6f616c90f526a8d6331b5e0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3664"/><div sID="gen5244" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3664"/><hi type="bold">24. The sons of Simeon--</hi>They are classed along with those of Judah, as their possession was partly taken out of the extensive territory of the latter (<reference osisRef="Josh.19.1">Jos 19:1</reference>). The difference in several particulars of the genealogy given here from that given in other passages is occasioned by some of the persons mentioned having more than one name [compare <reference osisRef="Gen.46.10">Ge 46:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.6.15">Ex 6:15</reference>; Nu 26:12]. <div eID="gen5244" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ed89dfa94bb37be02283345c757dff27c5ce668: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3665"/><div sID="gen5245" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3665"/><hi type="bold">27. his brethren had not many children--</hi>(see <reference osisRef="Num.1.22">Nu 1:22</reference>; 26:14). <div eID="gen5245" type="x-p"/>
entries.573fdb0fa8dc9b8ddc21d895bcc917784c59eebc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3666"/><div sID="gen5246" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3666"/><hi type="bold">31-43. These were their cities unto the reign of David--</hi>In consequence of the sloth or cowardice of the Simeonites, some of the cities within their allotted territory were only nominally theirs. They were never taken from the Philistines until David's time, when, the Simeonites having forfeited all claim to them, he assigned them to his own tribe of Judah (<reference osisRef="1Sam.27.6">1Sa 27:6</reference>). <div eID="gen5246" type="x-p"/>

entries.fe0cdf3afe12d6cc714a2ca79e6f139065210fdc: <div eID="gen13423" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13424" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13425" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13425" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13424" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13426" type="x-p"/> A second genealogy of Judah, vv. 1-23. The account of Jabez, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.9">1Chr 4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.10">1Chr 4:10</reference>. The genealogy of Simeon, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.24-1Chr.4.27">1Chr 4:24-27</reference>. Their cities, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.28-1Chr.4.31">1Chr 4:28-31</reference>. Their villages, and where situated, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.32">1Chr 4:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.33">1Chr 4:33</reference>. The heads of families, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.34-1Chr.4.38">1Chr 4:34-38</reference>. Where they settled; and what was their occupation, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.39-1Chr.4.43">1Chr 4:39-43</reference>. <div eID="gen13426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13427" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen13427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13428" type="x-p"/> The sons of Judah - A genealogy of this tribe has already been given in the second chapter. It is here introduced again, with some variations. Probably there were different copies in the public registers; and the writer of this book, finding that this second one contained some remarkable particulars, thought proper to insert it in this place: and no reader will regret the insertion, when he carefully considers the matter.
entries.370546fd4fe07f95d5eba78a5398e6681ae3436c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen13428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13429" type="x-p"/> These were of the father of Etam - "And these are the rabbins (doctors) living at Etam, Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash." - T.
entries.0d80f2c9b343086b69c7b4b0db0ed954f6fb607c: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen13429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13430" type="x-p"/> And Ethnan - After this word we should, with the Targum, read Coz, whose posterity is mentioned in the next verse. Coz was probably the same as Kenaz.
entries.6709391db6eef82b55d21e5825b5c99044836c26: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen13430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13431" type="x-p"/> The son of Harum - Jabez should be mentioned at the end of this verse, else he is as a consequent without an antecedent.
entries.938c9a675a69a4de047ebb111981656964488fb6: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen13431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13432" type="x-p"/> And Jabez was more honorable - This whole account is variously understood by some of the principal versions. I shall subjoin a translation of each. <div eID="gen13432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13433" type="x-p"/> Septuagint. - "And Igabes was more glorious than his brethren; and his mother called his name Igabes, saying, I have brought thee forth as Gabes. And Igabes invoked the God of Israel, saying, If in blessing thou wilt bless me, and enlarge my borders, and thy hand be with me, and wilt give me understanding not to depress me: and God brought about all that he requested." <div eID="gen13433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13434" type="x-p"/> Syriac. - "And one of these was dear to his father and to his mother; and he called his name ainai, My Eye. And he said to him, In blessing may the Lord bless thee, and enlarge thy boundary; and may his hand be with thee; and may he preserve thee from evil, that it may not rule over thee; and may he give to thee whatsoever thou shalt request of him!" <div eID="gen13434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13435" type="x-p"/> Arabic. - "And this one (Hastahar or Harum) was beloved of his father and his mother: and they called his name aina, My Eye; and they said unto him, May the Lord bless thee, and multiply thy people, and may his hand be present with thee, because thou wast born in Beth-lehem!" <div eID="gen13435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13436" type="x-p"/> These two latter versions seem to have copied each other, and the Vulgate is nearly, like ours, a literal rendering of the Hebrew; but the Chaldee is widely different from all the rest: - <div eID="gen13436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13437" type="x-p"/> Chaldee. - "And Jabets also, he is Othniel, honorable and skilled in the law beyond his brethren, whose mother called his name Jabets, because she had borne him with sorrow. And Jabets prayed to the God of Israel, saying, O that in blessing thou wouldest bless me with children, and enlarge my borders with disciples; and that thy hand may be with me in business, that thou mayest make me like to my companions, that evil concupiscence may the less grieve me! And the Lord granted that which he prayed for." <div eID="gen13437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13438" type="x-p"/> Of this honorable person we know nothing but what is here mentioned, nor does the name occur in any other part of Scripture except in <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.55">1Chr 2:55</reference>, where it appears to be the name of a place, but is understood by the Chaldee to be the name of a person, as here. Though I have noticed this particularly in the note on that place, yet I think it right to add the Chaldee here, that all that concerns this worthy person may be seen at one view: - <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.55">1Chr 2:55</reference> : "The families of the Rechabites, the son of Eliezer, the son of Moses, the disciples of Jabets; he was Othniel, the son of Kenaz. And he was called Jabets, יעבץ Yabets, because in his counsel [בעיצתיה beqtsatih, from יעץ yaats, he counselled, advised, etc.] he instituted a school for disciples. They were called Tirathim, תרעתים, because in their hymns their voices were like trumpets, [from רע ra, to sound like a trumpet; see <reference osisRef="Num.10.9">Num 10:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.12">2Chr 13:12</reference>], and Shimathim, שמעתים, because in hearing, they lifted up their faces, i.e. in prayer, [from שמע shama, he heard, hearkened], and Suchathim, שוכתים, because they were overshadowed with the spirit of prophecy, [from שך sach, a tabernacle, or extended covering]." For farther particulars, see at the end of this chapter, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.43">1Chr 4:43</reference> (note).
entries.b0526c2fa644bd414b536960f5d91f0a4736261a: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen13438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13439" type="x-p"/> These are the men of Rechah - "These are the men of the great Sanhedrin." - T.
entries.df6a34aed59baa03548ebad5629ebf984225d85c: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen13439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13440" type="x-p"/> Caleb the son of Jephunneh - We have already met with this eminent person in <reference osisRef="Num.13.6">Num 13:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.13.30">Num 13:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.14.24">Num 14:24</reference>, and elsewhere; and seen his courageous piety and inflexible integrity. The Targum says here, "They called him Caleb, the son of Jephunneh, because he had purged his soul from the counsel of the spies.
entries.fb6f6a8fdcdf139c15c8e2113f8602623ca07d12: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen13440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13441" type="x-p"/> And his wife Jehudijah - The Targum considers the names in this verse as epithets of Moses: "And his wife Jehuditha educated Moses after she had drawn him out of the water: and she called his name Jered, because he caused the manna to descend upon Israel; and Prince Gedor, because he restored the desolations of Israel; Heber also, because he joined Israel to their heavenly Father; and Prince Socho, because he overshadowed Israel with his righteousness, and Jekuthiel, because the Israelites waited on the God of heaven in his time, forty years in the desert; and prince Zanoah, because God, on his account, had passed by the sins of Israel. These names Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, called him by the spirit of prophecy, for she became a proselyte; and Mered took her to himself to wife: he is Caleb, and was so called because he opposed the counsel of the spies." - T. A similar explanation is given by Jarchi.
entries.e03db92d998b953541e9d54131baa96ce9ac5475: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen13441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13442" type="x-p"/> That wrought fine linen - "Of the family of those who worked in fine flax to make garments for kings and priests." - T.
entries.c180f90b6422f6a1c6f4a7b4048400b8b820db1d: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen13442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13443" type="x-p"/> And Joash, and Saraph - "And the prophets and scribes which sprang from the seed of Joshua, and the Gibeonites, whose office it was to serve in the house of the sanctuary, because they had lied to the princes of Israel; also Joash, who is the same as Mahlon; and Saraph, who is the same as Chilion, who took wives of the daughters of Moab and Boaz, the chief of the wise men of the college of Bethlehem, and of those who existed in former days." - T.
entries.56713d0b64a37332080ce50cb43bfacd2952850b: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen13443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13444" type="x-p"/> These were the potters - "These are the disciples of the law, for whose sake the world was created; who preside in judgment, and establish the world; and they build and perfect the fallen down house of Israel: they dwelt there with the Shechinah of the King of the world, in the study of the law and the intercalation or months, and determining the commencement of years and festivals: and they computed the times from heaven in the days of Ruth, the mother of kingdoms, to the days of Solomon the king." - T. I am afraid this paraphrase gives us as little light as the text itself, which speaks of potters, and those who dwelt among plants and hedges. They were probably brickmakers; perhaps potters also, who had their dwelling in low grounds, and fabricated the clay into pots and bricks that was digged up in forming fences in the king's domains.
entries.7853534475a4110cd0a87a4ece436e21c6ae313d: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen13444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13445" type="x-p"/> The sons of Simeon - This genealogy is very different from that given in <reference osisRef="Gen.46.10">Gen 46:10</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Num.26.12">Num 26:12</reference>. This may be occasioned by the same person having several names, one list taking one name, another list some other, and so on: to reconcile is impossible; to attempt it, useless.
entries.dd47c5780eb46f06682b996052f77881f8a04eb4: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen13445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13446" type="x-p"/> Neither did all their family multiply - In <reference osisRef="Num.1.23">Num 1:23</reference> the number of all the families of Simeon was fifty-nine thousand three hundred; and that of Judah was, <reference osisRef="Num.1.27">Num 1:27</reference>, not less than seventy-four thousand six hundred. When the next census was made, Num. 26, the tribe of Judah amounted to seventy-six thousand five hundred, an increase of one thousand nine hundred; while the tribe of Simeon amounted only to twenty-two thousand two hundred, a decrease of thirty-seven thousand one hundred. It was at that time the smallest tribe in Israel.
entries.7bb5ba2cd66263a7113b7b9a6661141b6c9a2af9: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen13446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13447" type="x-p"/> These were their cities unto the reign of David - It appears that David took some of the cities of the Simeonites, and added them to Judah; Ziklag for instance, <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.6">1Sam 27:6</reference>. <div eID="gen13447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13448" type="x-p"/> As the tribe of Simeon had withdrawn their allegiance from the house of David, the kings of Judah extended their domination as far as possible into the territories of that tribe, so that they were obliged to seek pasture for their flocks at Gedor, and in the mountains of Seir, as we find <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.39-1Chr.4.42">1Chr 4:39-42</reference>.
entries.4b26fd9c703e6c88a270837b2ab89db4cbb873f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen13448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13449" type="x-p"/> They of Ham had dwelt there of old - These were probably either Philistines or Egyptians, who dwelt at Gedor, which was situated in the environs of Joppa and Samnia. <div eID="gen13449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13450" type="x-p"/> Those whom the five hundred Simeonites expelled from Seir were Amalekites, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.43">1Chr 4:43</reference>.
entries.d00a45c1e7b14990978e4d068290ae562f8b10ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen13450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13451" type="x-p"/> They smote the rest of the Amalekites - Those who had escaped in the war which Saul made against them, (see <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.48">1Sam 14:48</reference>), and from David, who had attacked them afterwards, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.12">2Sam 8:12</reference>. <div eID="gen13451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13452" type="x-p"/> The expedition of the Simeonites mentioned here, against Gedor and Seir, was in the days of Hezekiah; and, as Calmet conjectures, near about the time of the captivity of the ten tribes, when the remnant of Simeon would feel themselves obliged to retire more southward, into Arabia Petraea, for fear of the Jews. These may be probable conjectures. - See Calmet. <div eID="gen13452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13453" type="x-p"/> There are several things in the account of Jabez that are very instructive: - <div eID="gen13453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13454" type="x-p"/> 1. He appears to have been a child brought into the world with great difficulty, at the risk of his own life and that of his mother. So much seems to be implied in, she bare him with sorrow, i.e., with peculiar sorrow and danger. <div eID="gen13454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13455" type="x-p"/> 2. To perpetuate the merciful interposition of God in her own and her son's behalf, she gave him a name that must have recalled to her and his remembrance the danger to which both their lives were exposed, and from which they could not have been extricated but by the especial help of God. She called his name Jabez, etc. <div eID="gen13455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13456" type="x-p"/> 3. He was brought up in the fear of God; he was no idolater; he worshipped the God of Israel, and he showed the sincerity of his faith by frequent and earnest prayer. <div eID="gen13456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13457" type="x-p"/> 4. His prayer was at once both enlightened and pious. He had piety towards God, and therefore he trusted in him: he knew that he was the fountain of all good, and therefore he sought all necessaries both for body and soul from him. He prayed to the God of Israel. <div eID="gen13457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13458" type="x-p"/> 5. Both the matter and manner of his prayer were excellent. His heart was deeply impressed with its wants, and therefore he was earnest and fervent; O that thou wouldest bless me indeed; אם ברך תברכני im barech tebarecheni; "O that in blessing thou wouldest bless me!" Let me live under thy benediction! Do thou diligently and frequently bless me! <div eID="gen13458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13459" type="x-p"/> 6. He prays for the things necessary for the body as well as for the soul: And enlarge my coasts - grant me as much territory as may support my family. Let the means of living be adequate to the demands of life; let me have the necessaries, conveniences, and, as far as they may be safely intrusted with me, the comforts of life! O that thou wouldest enlarge my coasts! <div eID="gen13459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13460" type="x-p"/> 7. He is conscious that without the continual support of God he must fail; and therefore he prays to be upheld by his power: That thy hand might be with me! May I ever walk with thee, and ever feel the hand of thy power to support and cover me in all the trials, dangers, and difficulties of life; and the hand of thy providence to supply all my wants in reference to both worlds! <div eID="gen13460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13461" type="x-p"/> 8. He dreads both sin and suffering, and therefore prays against both: O that thou wouldest keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me! Sin and misery are in every step of the journey of life; keep me from sin, that I grieve thee not; and keep me from sin, that I render not myself miserable! We can never offend God without injuring ourselves; he that sins must suffer. Thorns and scorpions are everywhere in the way to perdition; and he that walks in it must be torn and stung. He alone is happy who walks in the ways of God. Keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me. <div eID="gen13461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13462" type="x-p"/> 9. Prayers that have a right aim will have a right answer; Jabez did not pray in vain, for God granted him that which he requested. He was continually blessed; his family was increased; the hand of God was upon him for good. He was saved from sin, and saved from the pangs and sufferings of a guilty conscience. <div eID="gen13462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13463" type="x-p"/> 10. If we take up the character and conduct of Jabez in the view given by the Chaldee, we shall not only see him as a pious and careful man, deeply interested in behalf of himself and his family, but we shall see him as a benevolent man, laboring for the welfare of others, and especially for the religious instruction of youth. He founded schools, in which the young and rising generation were taught useful knowledge, and especially the knowledge of God. He had disciples, which were divided into three classes, who distinguished themselves by their fervor in the worship of God, by their docility in obediently hearing and treasuring up the advices and instructions of their teachers, and by their deep piety to God in bringing forth the fruits of the Spirit. The spirit of prophecy, that is, of prayer and supplication, rested upon them. <div eID="gen13463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13464" type="x-p"/> 11. He did not do these things merely as a duty he owed to God and his fellows, but from the abundance of a generous and loving heart: In his counsel he erected a school of disciples. God had blessed him with temporal things, and he secures their continuance by devoting them to his service; he honors God with his substance, and God honors him with his especial blessing and approbation. <div eID="gen13464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13465" type="x-p"/> 12. On these accounts he was more honorable than his brethren. He was of the same stock and the same lineage; he had neither nobility of birth, nor was distinguished by earthly titles; in all these respects he was on a level with his brethren: but God tells us that he was more honorable than them all; and why? because he prayed, because he served his Maker, and because he lived to do good among men; therefore he received the honor that cometh from God. Reader, imitate the conduct of this worthy Israelite, that thou mayest be a partaker of his blessings. <div eID="gen13465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13466" type="x-p"/> The things added by the Targumist might have been derived from authentic tradition.  <chapter eID="1Chr.4"/> <div eID="gen13466" type="x-p"/>

entries.ea56110e094f14f485f09a0745b1fc3e9388fcab: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.1">1Ch 4:1</reference> <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.1">1Ch 4:1</reference> is evidently intended to be a superscription to the genealogical fragments which follow. Five names are mentioned as sons of Judah, of whom only Pharez was his son (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.4">1Ch 2:4</reference>); the others are grandchildren or still more distant descendants. Nothing is said as to the genealogical relationship in which they stood to each other; that is supposed to be already known from the genealogies in 1 Chron 2. Hezron is the son of Pharez, and consequently grandson of Judah, 1Ch 2:8. Carmi, a descendant of Zerah, the brother of Pharez, see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.6">1Ch 2:6</reference>-7. Hur is a son of Caleb, the son of Hezron, by Ephratah (see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.19">1Ch 2:19</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.50">1Ch 2:50</reference>); and Shobal is the son of Hur, who has just been mentioned (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.50">1Ch 2:50</reference>). These five names do not denote here, any more than in 1 Chron 2, “families of the tribe of Judah” (Berth.), but signify persons who originated or were heads of families. The only conceivable ground for these five being called “sons of Judah,” is that the families registered in the following lists traced their origin to them, although in the enumeration which follows the genealogical connection of the various groups is not clearly brought out. The enumeration begins,
entries.7f2a2172a718f47989dd251709a85b34e651d3c6: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.2">1Ch 4:2</reference> <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.2">1Ch 4:2</reference>, with <hi type="italic">the descendants of Shobal</hi>. As to Reaiah the son of Shobal, see 1Ch 2:52. He begat Jahath, a name often occurring in Levite families, cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.5">1Ch 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.28">1Ch 6:28</reference>; 1Ch 23:10., <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.22">1Ch 24:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.12">2Ch 34:12</reference>; but of the descendant of David who bore this name nothing further is known. His sons Ahumai and Lahad founded the families of the Zorathites, i.e., the inhabitants of Zora, who also, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.53">1Ch 2:53</reference>, were descended from sons of Shobal. Our verse therefore gives more detailed information regarding the lineage of these families.
entries.e0345998adccdf1da9604d7261f44abe61753170: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.3">1Ch 4:3</reference> <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.3">1Ch 4:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.4">1Ch 4:4</reference> contain notices of the descendants of Hur. The first words of the third verse, “these, father of Etam, Jezreel,” have no meaning; but the last sentence of the second verse suggests that משׁפּחות should be supplied, when we read, “and these are the families of (from) Abi-Etam.” The lxx and Vulgate have עיטם בני אלה, which is also to be found in several codices, while other codices read בני אלה אבי עיטם. Both readings are probably only conjectures. Whether עיטם אבי is to be taken as the name of a person, or appellatively, father = lord of Etam, cannot be decided. עיטם is in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.32">1Ch 4:32</reference>, and probably also in Jdg 15:8, Jdg 15:11, the name of a town of the Simeonites; and in <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.6">2Ch 11:6</reference>, the name of a little town in the highlands of Judah, south of Jerusalem. If עיטם be the name of a place, only the lest named can be here meant. The names Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash denote persons as progenitors and head of families or branches of families. For יזרעאל as the name of a person, cf. Hos 1:4. That these names should be those of persons is required by the succeeding remark, “and their sister Hazelel-poni.” The formation of this name, with the derivative termination <hi type="italic">i</hi>, seems to express a relationship of race; but the word may also be an adjective, and as such may be a proper name: cf. Ew. §273, e.
entries.524765ad49347fbe00ef8f5e8acbf1fef9667b80: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.4">1Ch 4:4</reference> <div eID="gen5603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5604" type="x-p"/> Penuel, in Gen 32:31., Jdg 8:8, name of a place in the East-Jordan land, as here, and in Jdg 8:25 the name of a man. Gedor is, we may suppose, the town of that name in the mountains of Judah, which is still to be found in the ruin Jedur (see on <reference osisRef="Josh.15.58">Jos 15:58</reference>). Penuel is here called father of Bedor, while in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.18">1Ch 4:18</reference> one Jered is so called, whence we must conclude that the inhabitants of Gedor were descended from both. Ezer (Help) occurs in <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.21">1Ch 7:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.9">1Ch 12:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference>, of other men; father of Hushah, i.e., according to the analogy of Abi-Gedor, also the name of a place not elsewhere mentioned, where the hero Sibbecai had his birth, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.29">1Ch 11:29</reference>; 2Sa 23:27. Those thus named in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.3">1Ch 4:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.4">1Ch 4:4</reference> are sons of Hur, the first-born of Ephratah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.19">1Ch 2:19</reference>), the father of Bethlehem. The inhabitants of Bethlehem then, according to this, were descended from Hur through his son Salma, who is called in <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.51">1Ch 2:51</reference> father of Bethlehem. The circumstance, too, that in our <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.3">1Ch 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.4">1Ch 4:4</reference> other names of persons are enumerated as descendants of Hur than those given in <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.50-1Chr.2.55">1Ch 2:50-55</reference> gives rise to no discrepancy, for there is no ground for the supposition that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.50-1Chr.2.55">1Ch 2:50-55</reference> all the descendants of Hur have been mentioned.
entries.7351a8efc62c594a6b0a5e2dd3cec071586aac62: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.5-1Chr.4.6">1Ch 4:5-6</reference> <hi type="italic">Sons of Ashur</hi>, the father of Tekoa, who, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.24">1Ch 2:24</reference>, was a posthumous son of Hezron. Ashur had two wives, Helah and Naarah. Of the latter came four sons and as many families: Ahuzam, of whom nothing further is known; Hepher, also unknown, but to be distinguished from the Gileadite of the same name in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.36">1Ch 11:36</reference> and Num 26:32. The conjecture that the name is connected wit the land of Hepher (1Ki 4:10), the territory of a king conquered by Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.17">Jos 12:17</reference>) (Berth.), is not very well supported. Temani (man of the south) may be simply the name of a person, but it is probably, like the following, the name of a family. Haahashtari, descended from Ahashtar, is quite unknown.
entries.3eaa07ddaa5c95ab9d570343aac97cf98adaf81c: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.7">1Ch 4:7</reference> <div eID="gen5604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5605" type="x-p"/> The first wife, Helah, bore three sons, Zereth, Jezoar, and Ethnan, who are not elsewhere met with. For the Kethibh יצחר there is in the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> וצחר, the name of a son of Simeon (<reference osisRef="Gen.46.10">Gen 46:10</reference>), and of a Hittite chief in the time of the patriarchs (<reference osisRef="Gen.23.8">Gen 23:8</reference>), with whom the son of Helah has nothing to do.
entries.e55be00f5fd6c3348dd414dc1ae12497ceb4f82e: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.8-1Chr.4.10">1Ch 4:8-10</reference> <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.8-1Chr.4.10">1Ch 4:8-10</reference> contain a fragment, the connection of which with the sons of Judah mentioned in 1 Chron 2 is not clear. Coz begat Anub, etc. The name קוץ occurs only here; elsewhere only הקּוץ is found, of a Levite, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.10">1Ch 24:10</reference>, cf. Ezr 2:61 and <reference osisRef="Neh.3.4">Neh 3:4</reference> - in the latter passage without any statement as to the tribe to which the sons of Hakkoz belonged. The names of the sons begotten by Coz, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.8">1Ch 4:8</reference>, do not occur elsewhere. The same is to be said of Jabez, of whom we know nothing beyond what is communicated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.9">1Ch 4:9</reference> and 1Ch 4:10. The word יעבּץ denotes in <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.55">1Ch 2:55</reference> a town or village which is quite unknown to us; but whether our Jabez were father (lord) of this town cannot be determined. If there be any genealogical connection between the man Jabez and the locality of this name or its inhabitants (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.55">1Ch 2:55</reference>), then the persons named in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.8">1Ch 4:8</reference> would belong to the descendants of Shobal. For although the connection of Jabez with Coz and his sons is not clearly set forth, yet it may be conjectured from the statements as to Jabez being connected with the preceding by the words, “Jabez was more honoured than his brethren.” The older commentators have thence drawn the conclusion that Jabez was a son or brother of Coz. Bertheau also rightly remarks: “The statements that he was more honoured than his brethren (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.34.19">Gen 34:19</reference>), that his mother called him Jabez because she had borne him with sorrow; the use of the similarly sounding word עצב along with the name יעבּץ (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.4.25">Gen 4:25</reference>; Gen 19:37., <reference osisRef="Gen.29.32-Gen.29.33">Gen 29:32-33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.29.35">Gen 29:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.30.6">Gen 30:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.30.8">Gen 30:8</reference>, etc.); and the statement that Jabez vowed to the God of Israel (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.33.20">Gen 33:20</reference>) in a prayer (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.28.20">Gen 28:20</reference>), - all bring to our recollection similar statements of Genesis, and doubtless rest upon primeval tradition.” In the terms of the vow, עצבּי לבלתּי, “so that sorrow may not be to me,” there is a play upon the name Jabez. But of the vow itself only the conditions proposed by the maker of the vow are communicated: “If Thou wilt bless me, and enlarge my coast, and Thy hand shall be with me, and Thou wilt keep evil far off, not to bring sorrow to me,” - without the conclusion, Then I vow to do this or that (cf. Gen 28:20.), but with the remark that God granted him that which he requested. The reason of this is probably that the vow had acquired importance sufficient to make it worthy of being handed down only from God’s having so fulfilled his wish, that his life became a contradiction of his name; the son of sorrow having been free from pain in life, and having attained to greater happiness and reputation than his brothers.
entries.4e19241fb7ec8e382fdaeacac6328918f855c93d: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.11-1Chr.4.12">1Ch 4:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen5605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5606" type="x-p"/> The genealogy of the men of Rechah. - As to their connection with the larger families of Judah, nothing has been handed down to us. Chelub, another form of the name Caleb or Chelubai (see <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.9">1Ch 2:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.18">1Ch 2:18</reference>), is distinguished from the better known Caleb son of Hezron (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.18">1Ch 2:18</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.42">1Ch 2:42</reference>), and from the son of Jephunneh (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.15">1Ch 4:15</reference>), by the additional clause, “the son of Shuah.” Shuah is not met with elsewhere, but is without reason identified with Hushah, <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.4">1Ch 4:4</reference>, by the older commentators. Mehir the father of Eshton is likewise unknown. Eshton begat the house (the family) of Rapha, of whom also nothing further is said; for they can be connected neither with the Benjamite Rapha (<reference osisRef="1Chr.8.2">1Ch 8:2</reference>) nor with the children of Rapha (<reference osisRef="1Chr.20.4">1Ch 20:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.6">1Ch 20:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.8">1Ch 20:8</reference>). Paseah and Tehinnah are also unknown, for it is uncertain whether the sons of Paseah mentioned among the Nethinim, Ezr 2:49; <reference osisRef="Neh.7.51">Neh 7:51</reference>, have any connection with our Paseah. Tehinnah is called “father of the city of Nahash.” The latter name is probably not properly the name of a town, but rather the name of a person Nahash, not unlikely the same as the father of Abigail (<reference osisRef="2Sam.17.25">2Sa 17:25</reference>), the step-sister of David (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.16">1Ch 2:16</reference>). The men (or people) of Rechah are unknown.
entries.98ed0ee94d731f710084011a611f22f97e64e17e: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.13-1Chr.4.14">1Ch 4:13-14</reference> <hi type="italic">Descendants of Kenaz.</hi> - קנז is a descendant of Hezron the son of Pharez, as may be inferred from the fact that Caleb the son of Jephunneh, a descendant of Hezron’s son Caleb, is called in Num 32:12 and <reference osisRef="Josh.14.6">Jos 14:6</reference> קנזּי, and consequently was also a descendant of Kenaz. Othniel and Seraiah, introduced here as קנז בּני, are not sons (in the narrower sense of the word), but more distant descendants of Kenaz; for Othniel and Caleb the son of Jephunneh were, according to <reference osisRef="Josh.15.17">Jos 15:17</reference> and Jdg 1:13, brothers.<note placement="foot">The words used in Jdg 1:13, cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.15.17">Jos 15:17</reference>, of the relationship of Othniel and Caleb, הקּטון כלב אחי בּן־קנז, may be, it is true, taken in different senses, either as signifying <hi type="italic">filius Kenasi fratris Caleb</hi>, according to which, not Othniel, but Kenaz, was a younger brother of Caleb; or in this way, <hi type="italic">filius Kenasi, frater Calebi minor</hi>, as we have interpreted them in the text, and also in the commentary on Jos 15:17. This interpretation we still hold to be certainly the correct one, notwithstanding what Bachmann (<hi type="italic">Buch der Richter,</hi> on <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.13">1Ch 1:13</reference>) has brought forward against it and in favour of the other interpretation, and cannot see that his chief reasons are decisive. The assertion that we must predicate of Othniel, if he be a younger brother of Caleb, an unsuitably advanced age, is not convincing. Caleb was eighty-five years of age at the division of the land of Canaan (<reference osisRef="Josh.14.10">Jos 14:10</reference>). Now if we suppose that his younger or youngest brother Othniel was from twenty-five to thirty years younger, as often happens, Othniel would be from sixty to sixty-one or fifty-five to fifty-six years of age at the conquest of Debir, - an age at which he might well win a wife as the reward of valour. Ten years later came the invasion of the land by Cushan Rishathaim, which lasted eight years, till Othniel had conquered Cushan R., and there were judges in Israel. This victory he would thus gain at the age of seventy-eight or seventy-three; and even if he filled the office of judge for forty years-which, however, Jdg 3:11 does not state - he would have reached no greater age than 118 or 113 years, only three or eight years older than Joshua had been. If we consider what Caleb said of himself in his eighty-fifth year, <reference osisRef="Josh.14.11">Jos 14:11</reference>, “I am still strong as in the day that Moses sent me (i.e., forty years before); as my strength was then, even so is my strength now for war, both to go out and to come in,” we cannot think that Othniel, in the seventy-third or seventy-eighth years of his age, was too old to be a military leader. But the other reason: “that Caleb is always called son of Jephunneh, Othniel always son of Kenaz, should cause us to hesitate before we take Othniel to be the proper brother of Caleb,” loses all its weight when we find that Caleb also is called in Num 32:12 and <reference osisRef="Josh.14.6">Jos 14:6</reference> קנזי = בּן־קנז, and it is seen that Caleb therefore, as well as Othniel, was a son of Kenaz. Now if the Kenazite Caleb the son of Jephunneh were a brother of Kenaz, the father of Othniel, we must suppose an older Kenaz, the grandfather or great-grandfather of Caleb, and a younger Kenaz, the father of Othniel. This supposition is certainly feasible, for, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.15">1Ch 4:15</reference> of our chapter, a grandson of Caleb again was called Kenaz; but if it be probable is another question. For the answering of this question in the affirmative, Bachmann adduces that, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.13">1Ch 4:13</reference>, Othniel is undoubtedly the son of Kenaz in the proper sense of the word; but it might perhaps be difficult to prove, or even to render probable, this “undoubtedly.” In the superscriptions of the single genealogies of the Chronicle, more than elsewhere, בּני has in general a very wide signification. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.1">1Ch 4:1</reference> of our chapter, for instance, sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons of Judah are all grouped together as יהוּדה בּני. But besides this, the ranging of the sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.15">1Ch 4:15</reference>) after the enumeration of the sons of Kenaz in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.13">1Ch 4:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.14">1Ch 4:14</reference>, is clearly much more easily explicable if Caleb himself belonged to the קנז בּני mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.13">1Ch 4:13</reference>, than if he was a brother of Kenaz. In the latter case we should expect, after the analogy of <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.42">1Ch 2:42</reference>, to find an additional clause קנז אחי after בּן־יפנּה כּלב; while if Caleb was a brother of Othniel, his descent from Kenaz, or the fact that he belonged to the קנז בּני, might be assumed to be known from Num 32:12.</note> <div eID="gen5606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5607" type="x-p"/> Kenaz, therefore, can neither have been the father of Othniel nor father of Caleb (in the proper sense of the word), but must at least have been the grandfather or great-grandfather of both. Othniel is the famous first judge of Israel, Jdg 3:9. Of Seraiah nothing further is known, although the name is often met with of different persons. <div eID="gen5607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5608" type="x-p"/> The sons of Othniel are Hathath. The plural בּני, even when only one name follows, is met with elsewhere (<hi type="italic">vide</hi> on <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.7">1Ch 2:7</reference>); but the continuation is somewhat strange, “and Meonothai begat Ophrah,” for as Meonothai is not before mentioned, his connection with Othniel is not given. There is evidently a hiatus in the text, which may most easily be filled up by repeating וּמעונתי at the end of 1Ch 4:13. According to this conjecture two sons of Othniel would be named, Hathath and Meonothai, and then the posterity of the latter is given. The name מעונתי (my dwellings) is not met with elsewhere. It is not at all probable that it is connected with the town Maon, and still less that it is so in any way with the Mehunim, Ezr 2:50. Ophrah is unknown, for of course we must not think of the towns called Ophrah, in the territory of Benjamin, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.23">Jos 18:23</reference>, and in that of Manasseh, Jdg 6:11, Jdg 6:24. Seraiah, who is mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.13">1Ch 4:13</reference>, begat Joab the father (founder) of the valley of the craftsmen, “for they (i.e., the inhabitants of this valley, who were descended from Joab) were craftsmen.” The valley of the חרשׁים (craftsmen) is again mentioned in <reference osisRef="Neh.11.35">Neh 11:35</reference>, whence we may conclude that it lay at no great distance from Jerusalem, in a northern direction.
entries.be254f7ee695cfdcc461906f3b5317fee7a317d4: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.15">1Ch 4:15</reference> <div eID="gen5608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5609" type="x-p"/> Of Iru, Elah, and Naam, the sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh (cf. on <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.13">1Ch 4:13</reference>), nothing more is known. To connect Elah with the Edomite chief of that name (<reference osisRef="1Chr.1.52">1Ch 1:52</reference>) is arbitrary. Of Elah’s sons only “and Kenaz” is mentioned; the ו copul. before קנז shows clearly that a name has been dropped out before it.<hi type="italic">Descendants of various men</hi>, whose genealogical connection with the sons and grandsons of Judah, mentioned in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.1">1Ch 4:1</reference>, is not given in the text as it has come to us.
entries.3a4c18eb95038702a31062c7ee66a5a77c5971a2: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.16">1Ch 4:16</reference> <div eID="gen5609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5610" type="x-p"/> Sons of Jehaleleel, a man not elsewhere mentioned. Ziph, Ziphah, etc., are met with only here. There is no strong reason for connecting the name זיף with the towns of that name, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.24">Jos 15:24</reference>, Jos 15:55.
entries.5d266c93781b1178450d1a61588ad1a173527d06: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.17-1Chr.4.19">1Ch 4:17-19</reference> <div eID="gen5610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5611" type="x-p"/> Ezra, whose four sons are enumerated, is likewise unknown. The singular בּן is peculiar, but has analogies in <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.19">1Ch 3:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.3.21">1Ch 3:21</reference>, and 1Ch 3:23. Of the names of his sons, Jether and Epher again occur, the former in <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.53">1Ch 2:53</reference>, and the latter in <reference osisRef="1Chr.1.33">1Ch 1:33</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.5.24">1Ch 5:24</reference>, but in other families. Jalon, on the contrary, is found only here. The children of two wives of Mered are enumerated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.17">1Ch 4:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.18">1Ch 4:18</reference>, but in a fashion which is quite unintelligible, and shows clear traces of a corruption in the text. For (1) the name of a woman as subject of ותּהר, “and she conceived (bare),” is wanting; and (2) in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.18">1Ch 4:18</reference> the names of two women occur, Jehudijah and Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh. But the sons of Jehudijah are first given, and there follows thereupon the formula, “and these are the sons of Bithiah,” without any mention of the names of these sons. This manifest confusion Bertheau has sought to remove by a happy transposition of the words. He suggests that the words, “and these are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered had taken,” should be placed immediately after וילון. “By this means we obtain (1) the missing subject of ותּהר;   (2) the definite statement that Mered had two wives, with whom he begat sons; and (3) an arrangement by which the sons are enumerated after the names of their respective mothers.” After this transposition the <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.17">1Ch 4:17</reference> would read thus: “And the sons of Ezra are Jether, Mered, ... and Jalon; and these are the sons of Bithia the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took; and she conceived (and bare) Miriam, and Shammai, and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa (<reference osisRef="1Chr.4.18">1Ch 4:18</reference>), and his wife Jehudijah bore Jered the father of Gedor, etc.” This conjecture commends itself by its simplicity, and by the clearness which it brings into the words. From them we then learn that two families, who dwelt in a number of the cities of Judah, were descended from Mered the son of Ezra by his two wives. We certainly know no more details concerning them, as neither Mered not his children are met with elsewhere. From the circumstance, however, that the one wife was a daughter of Pharaoh, we may conclude that Mered lived before the Exodus of the Israelites from Egypt. The name Miriam, which Moses’ sister bore, is here a man’s name. The names introduced by אבי are the names of towns. Ishbah is father (lord) of the town Eshtemoa, in the mountains of Judah, now Semua, a village to the south of Hebron, with considerable ruins dating from ancient times (cf. on <reference osisRef="Josh.15.50">Jos 15:50</reference>). היהוּדיּה means properly “the Jewess,” as distinguished from the Egyptian woman, Pharaoh’s daughter. Gedor is a town in the high lands of Judah (cf. on <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.4">1Ch 4:4</reference>). Socho, in the low land of Judah, now Shuweikeh, in Wady Sumt (cf. on <reference osisRef="Josh.15.35">Jos 15:35</reference>). Zanoah is the name of a town in the high lands of Judah, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.56">Jos 15:56</reference> (which has not yet been discovered), and of a town in the low land, now Zanua, not far from Zoreah, in an easterly direction (cf. on <reference osisRef="Josh.15.34">Jos 15:34</reference>). Perhaps the latter is here meant<hi type="italic">.</hi> In <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.19">1Ch 4:19</reference>, “the sons of the wife of Hodiah, the sister of Naham, are the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite.” The stat. contr. אשׁת before הודיּה shows that Hodiah is a man’s name. Levites of this name are mentioned in <reference osisRef="Neh.8.7">Neh 8:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.5">Neh 9:5</reference>; Neh 10:11. The relationship of Hodiah and Naham to the persons formerly named is not given. קעילה is a locality in the low land of Judah not yet discovered (see on <reference osisRef="Josh.15.44">Jos 15:44</reference>). The origin of the Epithet הגּרמי we do not know. Before אשׁתּמע, אבי with ו copul. is probably to be repeated; and the Maachathite, the chief of a part of the inhabitants of Eshtemoa, is perhaps a descendant of Caleb by Maachah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.48">1Ch 2:48</reference>).
entries.043272652f6e2a9cd11209a8877905cc3f8d487b: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.20">1Ch 4:20</reference> <div eID="gen5611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5612" type="x-p"/> Of Shimon and his four sons, also, nothing is known. בּן־חנן is one name. Ishi is often met with, e.g., <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.42">1Ch 4:42</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.31">1Ch 2:31</reference>, but nowhere in connection with Zoheth (not further noticed). The names of the sons are wanting after בּן־זוחת.
entries.33f5a569cb67adac13bd83ededea18c16640710a: <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.21-1Chr.4.22">1Ch 4:21-22</reference> <hi type="italic">Descendants of Shelah</hi>, the third son of Judah, <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.3">1Ch 2:3</reference>, and Gen 38:5. - All the families of Judah enumerated in vv. 2-20 are connected together by the conjunction ו, and so are grouped as descendants of the sons and grandsons of Judah named in 1Ch 4:1. The conjunction is omitted, however, before שׁלה בּני, as also before יהוּדה בּני in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.3">1Ch 4:3</reference>, to show that the descendants of Shelah form a second line of descendants of Judah, co-ordinate with the sons of Judah enumerated in vv. 1-19, concerning whom only a little obscure but not unimportant information has been preserved. Those mentioned as sons are Er (which also was the name of the first-born of Judah, 1Ch 2:3.), father of Lecah, and Laadan, the father of Mareshah. The latter name denotes, beyond question, a town which still exists as the ruin Marash in the <hi type="italic">Shephelah</hi>, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.44">Jos 15:44</reference> (see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.42">1Ch 2:42</reference>), and consequently Lecah (לכה) also is the name of a locality not elsewhere mentioned. The further descendants of Shelah were, “the families of the Byssus-work of the house of Ashbea,” i.e., the families of Ashbea, a man of whom nothing further is known. Of these families some were connected with a famous weaving-house or linen (Byssus) manufactory, probably in Egypt; and then further, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.4.22">1Ch 4:22</reference>, “Jokim, and the man of Chozeba, and Joash, and Saraph, which ruled over Moab, and Jashubi-lehem.” Kimchi conjectured that כּזבה was the place called כזיב in <reference osisRef="Gen.38.5">Gen 38:5</reference> = אכזיב, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.44">Jos 15:44</reference>, in the low land, where Shelah was born. לחם ישׁבי is a strange name, “which the punctuators would hardly have pronounced in the way they have done if it had not come down to them by tradition” (Berth.).
